t.4.1: Then Kāma's wife, who had sunk into a swoon and lay helpless, was brought back to consciousness by Fate, which meant to make her suffer a fresh widowhood whose pain was unbearable.
t.4.2: Opening her eyes at the end of her swoon, she made them intent and watchful; she did not know that the beloved, dear to those unsated eyes, had passed forever beyond their sight.
t.4.4: Then she, overwhelmed once more, her breasts grey with dust from embracing the earth and her hair dishevelled, lamented, as though making the very ground share her grief.
t.4.3: Crying, “Ah, lord of my life, are you alive?”, she rose, and there before her on the ground she saw nothing but the ashes of the fire of Hara's wrath, still in the shape of a man.
t.4.5: That body of yours which, through its radiant beauty, was the very standard of comparison for all gallant lovers has now come to such a state, and yet I do not break apart; women are hard-hearted indeed.
t.4.6: Where have you fled, your affection broken in an instant, casting me aside, me whose very life depends on you, as a mass of water that has burst its dam rushes away and abandons the lotus pond?
t.4.7: You have done me no wrong, nor have I done anything against you. Why, then, without any cause, is the sight of you not granted to Rati as she laments?
t.4.8: Do you remember, Smara, how I bound you with the cords of my girdle whenever you slipped and called me by another woman's name? Or the blows I struck with the lotus from my ear, whose falling pollen stung your eyes?
t.4.9: The pleasing words you spoke to me, 'You dwell in my heart,' I now know to have been deceit; for if this were not a mere phrase of courtesy, how is it that you are bodiless while Rati remains unharmed?
t.4.10: I shall follow the path of you who have just set out on your journey to the other world; this person has been cheated by fate, for the happiness of embodied beings depends on you alone.
t.4.11: When the city's roads are veiled in the darkness of night, and beloved women tremble at the rumbling of the clouds, who but you, my beloved, has the power to lead them to the dwellings of their lovers?
t.4.12: Now that you are gone, the intoxication of wine, which rolls the reddened eyes and makes words stumble at every step, is a mere mockery for young women.
t.4.13: Having learned that the body of you, his dear friend, has been reduced to a mere tale, the moon, whose rising is now fruitless, will only with difficulty cast off his thinness, O Anaṅga, even when the dark fortnight has passed.
t.4.14: Tell me, whose arrow will the fresh mango blossom now become, with its lovely stalk of green and red, its coming announced by the sweet call of the male cuckoo?
t.4.15: This row of bees, which you so many times employed to serve as the string of your bow, seems with its humming cries of piteous sound to weep along with me, heavy with grief.
t.4.16: Rise up now, take on once more your captivating form, and appoint the cuckoo, by nature skilled in sweet speech, to the offices of Rati's messenger.
t.4.17: Remember those embraces of yours, begged for as you bowed your head to the ground, and full of trembling, and those lovemakings in secret; recalling them, I find no peace.
t.4.18: O you who are skilled in the art of love, this seasonal adornment of flowers, which you yourself arranged upon my limbs, is still worn, yet that lovely body of yours is seen no more.
t.4.19: You were summoned by the cruel gods while the adorning of this foot was still unfinished; come, make this left foot of mine complete with its red lac.
t.4.20: Following the path of the moth into the flame, I shall come to you and once again rest upon your lap, beloved, before you are seduced in heaven by the clever women of the gods.
t.4.21: "Rati, bereft of Madana, lived on, they say, for even a moment": this reproach is now fixed upon me, my beloved, even if I follow you.
t.4.22: How am I to give you the last adornment, now that the other world has taken you from me? For you have passed to an unimagined fate with your body and your life at one and the same time.
t.4.23: I remember you, your bow resting in your lap as you straightened your arrow, and your smiling talk with Madhu, and that glance you cast from the corner of your eye.
t.4.25: Then Madhu, pierced in the heart by those words of lament as if by poisoned arrows, revealed himself before the stricken Rati in order to console her.
t.4.24: Where now is Madhu, your dear friend who touched your heart, he who fitted flowers to your bow? Surely Pinākin, in his fierce wrath, has not sent him too along the path his friend has gone?
t.4.26: Seeing him, she wept bitterly and beat her bosom, crowded close by her breasts; for in the presence of one's own people, grief comes forth as though a door had been thrown open.
t.4.27: And grief-stricken, she spoke to him thus: "Vasanta, see what remains of your friend: this ash, mottled like a dove's wing, that the winds scatter grain by grain."
t.4.28: Ah, Smara, show yourself now; this Mādhava longs to see you. The love of men may be unsteady toward their beloved women, but surely it is not fickle toward a friend.
t.4.29: Surely it was with this companion at your side that the whole world, gods and asuras alike, was made to obey the command of your bow, whose string is a lotus-fiber and whose arrows are delicate flowers.
t.4.30: Your friend is gone and does not return, like a lamp extinguished by the wind; and I am like its wick: look at me, blackened by unbearable calamity.
t.4.31: Surely Fate has wrought only half the slaughter, sparing me when Kāma was slain; for when the tree that was its support is broken by an elephant, the creeper, though blameless, is bound to fall.
t.4.33: Moonlight departs together with the moon; lightning vanishes together with the cloud. That women follow the path of their husbands is acknowledged even by things devoid of sense.
t.4.32: So let this duty of a kinsman be performed by you without delay: by consigning me, forlorn as I am, to the fire, bring me, I pray, to my husband's side.
t.4.34: With my breasts tinged by this very ash, so lovely, from my beloved's body, I shall lay my body upon the fire as though upon a bed of fresh young shoots.
t.4.35: Gentle one, you have often given the two of us your help in spreading a couch of flowers; now, implored by me with hands folded in supplication, quickly make for me a funeral pyre.
t.4.36: Then, with fannings of the southern breeze, you should quicken the fire to which I have been offered; for surely it is known to you that Smara cannot bear to be even a moment without me.
t.4.37: And having done this, let a single handful of water be offered for the two of us; that friend of yours, together with me, will drink it in the other world without dividing it.
t.4.38: And in the rites for the other world, O Mādhava, offer to Smara clusters of mango blossoms with trembling young shoots, for your friend was fond of mango flowers.
t.4.39: As Rati stood thus, resolved on release from life for the sake of her lord, a voice born of the sky took pity on her, as the first rain takes pity on a little fish distressed by the drying of its pool.
t.4.40: O wife of the flower-armed god, your husband will not long remain beyond your reach. Hear now by what deed he became a moth in the flame of Hara's eye.
t.4.42: When Hara, drawn toward her by her austerity, weds Pārvatī, then, having found happiness, he will restore Smara to his own body.
t.4.41: Prajāpati, his senses aroused, conceived a desire for his own daughter; then, once he had restrained that agitation, Kāma, cursed by him, has reaped this fruit.
t.4.44: Therefore, O lovely one, preserve this body of yours, which is destined to meet again with your beloved; for a river whose waters have been drunk up by the sun is once more joined with its flood when the hot season has passed.
t.4.46: Then the wife of Madana, wasted by her grief, waited for the end of her calamity, as the crescent of the daytime moon, grey with the loss of its rays, waits for the evening.
t.4.45: Thus some being of invisible form weakened Rati's resolve to die; and, trusting in that voice, the friend of the flower-weaponed god comforted her with words whose phrases were apt and full of meaning.
t.4.43: And he, entreated by Dharma, spoke these words, which set a limit to the curse on Smara: "The self-controlled and the rain-clouds are the sources of both the thunderbolt and the nectar."
